claims.text: Luke names Annas and Caiaphas as high priests, and John says Annas was Caiaphas's father-in-law.
Josephus says the governor Valerius Gratus removed Ananus, then appointed and removed Ismael, Eleazar and Simon, after which Joseph Caiaphas was made high priest.
According to Josephus, Caiaphas was appointed in AD 18, and his eighteen-year tenure was comparatively long.
Gratus stayed eleven years in Judea; then Pontius Pilate came as his successor.
Josephus says the high priest's vestments were kept in the tower of Antonia until Vitellius allowed the priests to have custody of them again.
Josephus says Ananus, widely identified with the Annas of the Gospels, had five sons who all served as high priest.
In Matthew, Jesus overturned the tables of the money changers in the Temple.
In John, after the raising of Lazarus the chief priests and Pharisees gathered the council, fearing that the Romans would come and take away both their place and their nation.
In John, Caiaphas told them they knew nothing at all, and that it was better for them that one man should die for the people than that the whole nation perish.
Josephus says two thousand of the rebels were crucified after the revolt that followed Herod the Great's death.
Matthew says the chief priests and elders met in the court of the high priest, named Caiaphas, and planned to seize Jesus secretly, not during the feast, for fear of a riot.
John says Jesus was bound and taken first to Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas.
Mark says many bore false witness against Jesus, but their testimonies did not agree.
Caiaphas asked Jesus whether he was the Christ, the Son of God; Matthew has Jesus answer 'You have said so', while Mark has him answer 'I am'.
The high priest tore his clothes, said Jesus had blasphemed, and the council answered that he deserved death.
While this went on, Peter sat in the courtyard and denied Jesus three times.
The Gospels do not tell the night of the hearing the same way: Matthew places it in Caiaphas's house, Mark says only 'to the high priest', and John has Annas question Jesus first.
claims.note: The accounts differ and scholars debate how to reconcile them.

claims.text: John says the priests took Jesus to Pilate early in the morning and told him it was not lawful for them to put anyone to death.
Luke says the priests accused Jesus before Pilate of claiming to be a king, and John has them cry out 'We have no king but Caesar'.
Matthew says the chief priests asked Pilate for a guard at the tomb and, when the tomb was empty, paid the soldiers to say the disciples had stolen the body.
Acts lists Annas the high priest and Caiaphas among those who questioned Peter and John.
In Acts, the Pharisee Gamaliel urged the council to leave the apostles alone: if their work was from men it would fail, but if it was from God they could not stop it.
Josephus says Vitellius deprived Joseph, also called Caiaphas, of the high priesthood and appointed Jonathan, son of Ananus.
In November 1990, workers found an ornate limestone ossuary in the Peace Forest south of Abu Tor in Jerusalem, inscribed in Aramaic with what was read as 'Joseph son of Caiaphas'.
Some scholars have challenged the identification of the 1990 ossuary as that of the high priest, citing the spelling of the inscription and the lack of any mention of his rank.
claims.note: Identification disputed; the ossuary is ornate, but the tomb was plain.

claims.text: In 2011 archaeologists announced a recovered ossuary inscribed 'Miriam, daughter of Yeshua, son of Caiaphas, Priest of Ma'aziah from Beth 'Imri', which the Israel Antiquities Authority declared authentic.
Josephus complains that high priests sent servants to the threshing floors to take the tithes due the ordinary priests, so that the poorest priests died for want.

The Second Vatican Council's Nostra aetate (1965), addressing the question of Jewish culpability for the trial and crucifixion of Jesus, says that what happened in Christ's passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then alive, nor against the Jews of today.
In his Inferno, Dante places Caiaphas among the hypocrites in the eighth circle of Hell.

paragraphs.text: Under Roman rule, high priests rose and fell like the seasons. Josephus lists them: one removed, another appointed, then removed in turn.
Caiaphas was the exception. He held the office for eighteen years, and those years include the night Jesus was brought before him.
Was he a villain, or a political survivor doing cold arithmetic in an occupied country? Tonight we look at what the sources actually say.

Start with how little power the office really had. Josephus says the high priest's sacred vestments were kept in the tower of Antonia, the citadel beside the Temple, until the governor Vitellius let the priests take them back.

The governor before Pilate, Valerius Gratus, treated the job like a revolving door. Josephus says he removed Ananus, appointed Ismael, removed him, then Eleazar, then Simon, and only then Joseph Caiaphas. The year was AD 18.

Caiaphas had the best connection available. John says he was the son-in-law of Annas, and Josephus adds that Ananus, the man most scholars identify with Annas, had five sons who all served as high priest. This was not luck. It was a family business.
And Annas never really left. Luke names both men as high priests in the same breath. Many historians see Annas as the power in the background and Caiaphas as the man out front.
Gratus stayed eleven years, then Pontius Pilate arrived. Caiaphas stayed too. Historians read that long tenure as a sign of a working relationship with Rome.

script.heading: The road to the night hearing

paragraphs.text: Then Jesus walked into the Temple and overturned the tables of the money changers, the very marketplace the high-priestly families oversaw. To the priests it must have looked less like a sermon than a challenge.

The turning point, in John's Gospel, comes after Jesus raises Lazarus. The chief priests and Pharisees gather the council in alarm: if we let him go on, they say, the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation.
Caiaphas answers bluntly. You know nothing at all, he says. It is better for you that one man die for the people than that the whole nation perish.

Read coldly, that is not a speech about hatred. It is arithmetic. Josephus says two thousand rebels were crucified after the revolt that followed Herod the Great's death. That is the backdrop to his arithmetic.
Matthew says the chief priests and elders met in the court of the high priest, named Caiaphas, to seize Jesus quietly. Not during the feast, they said, or there may be a riot.
That night Jesus was arrested. John says he was bound and taken first to Annas, the father-in-law of Caiaphas.
From there he was led to Caiaphas's house, where, Matthew says, the scribes and elders were already gathered.

script.heading: The night hearing and what the sources say

paragraphs.text: Witnesses were brought in. Mark says many spoke against him, but their testimonies did not agree. Jesus, for much of it, said nothing.
Then Caiaphas asked him directly: are you the Christ, the Son of God? In Matthew, Jesus answers, you have said so. In Mark, he answers, I am. Either way, it was enough.
The high priest tore his clothes and declared it blasphemy. The council answered that Jesus deserved death.
Meanwhile, in the courtyard outside, Peter was warming himself by a fire, and denying three times that he had ever known the prisoner inside.

Even here the sources disagree. Matthew puts the hearing in Caiaphas's house, Mark says only that Jesus was taken to the high priest, and John has Annas question him first. Historians still argue over how the accounts fit together.
At dawn the priests took Jesus to Pilate. John says they told him it was not lawful for them to put anyone to death.

Before Pilate the charge changes. Blasphemy meant nothing to Rome, so Luke has the priests claim that Jesus called himself a king. And in John they cry out: we have no king but Caesar. Exactly what a man who needs Rome's goodwill would say.
Matthew adds a coda. The chief priests asked Pilate for a guard at the tomb. And when the tomb was found empty, Matthew says, they paid the soldiers to claim the disciples had stolen the body.
Caiaphas appears again in Acts. When Peter and John are arrested for preaching in the Temple, Acts lists who questioned them: Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, and others of the high-priestly family.
Some on the council wanted the apostles killed. A Pharisee named Gamaliel urged caution: if this is from men, it will fail on its own, and if it is from God, you cannot stop it.

Then, abruptly, it was over. Josephus says the Syrian governor Vitellius came to Jerusalem, handed the priests back custody of the sacred vestments, and deprived Joseph Caiaphas of the high priesthood, appointing Jonathan, a son of Ananus.

A man who survived eighteen years and two governors was removed in a single visit. In that passage Josephus gives no reason and does not say where he went. The priest at the center of history's most famous trial simply disappears from the page.
Then, in November 1990, workers paving a road in Jerusalem's Peace Forest, south of the Abu Tor neighborhood, found an ornate limestone ossuary, a box for bones.
On its side was an Aramaic inscription read as Joseph son of Caiaphas. Inside were the bones of an elderly man.

Is it him? Some scholars say yes. Others challenge it, pointing to the spelling of the inscription and the lack of any mention that this Joseph was high priest. The evidence is suggestive, not settled.

A second find points the same way. In 2011, archaeologists announced a recovered ossuary inscribed Miriam, daughter of Yeshua, son of Caiaphas, Priest of Ma'aziah, which the Israel Antiquities Authority declared authentic.
So what kind of man was he? One reading says he feared Jesus as a threat to his own power. John's council does fear losing its place.

A second reading is political, not personal: a man keeping a fragile peace in an occupied province, where one riot could bring legions. He did not need to hate Jesus. He only needed to believe disorder was deadlier than one man's death. Both readings fit the evidence.

Priestly dynasties did not have a good reputation. Josephus complains that high priests sent their servants to the threshing floors to take the tithes due the ordinary priests, until the poorest priests died for want.

That context matters for how the story was later used. In 1965 the Second Vatican Council, addressing the question of Jewish culpability for Jesus's trial and crucifixion, said in Nostra aetate that what happened in Christ's passion cannot be charged against all the Jews then alive, nor against the Jews of today.
In literature he fared worse. Dante's Inferno places Caiaphas among the hypocrites, in the eighth circle of Hell. A medieval verdict, not a historical one.

So who was Caiaphas? A high priest who lasted eighteen years in a job Rome made nearly impossible to keep. A politician who judged one man's death cheaper than a nation's. And a name that may have survived on a limestone box. Villain or realist, the evidence lets us ask, but not settle it.
